title: Gold doesn’t move in size unless something is star...
content:
Gold doesn’t move in size unless something is starting to crack. And to be clear, the chart is showing gold leaving the United States..non monetary gold exports recorded in U.S. trade data. That matters. But countries don’t move physical gold around because they’re making a clever trade or chasing returns. They do it when there’s concern about currency stability, access to the financial system, or whether the plumbing will still work when stress hits. Gold is what gets moved when trust starts to fade.
When foreign currencies come under pressure from inflation, debt loads, politics, capital controls, or sanctions risk..large institutions and central banks start shifting out of paper claims into assets that don’t require permission. Gold fits that role almost perfectly. It doesn’t rely on another central bank, another legal system, or a clearing network that can be frozen or politicized. That’s why it becomes more attractive precisely when confidence in local money starts slipping.
This is all happening in a world where the dollar still sits at the center, but where access to the system feels more conditional than it used to. Sanctions, asset freezes, and financial leverage have changed how countries think about reserves. Even allies are more careful now. They want assets that are portable, neutral, and hard to interfere with. Gold checks those boxes..so when risk rises, it isn’t just bought, it’s physically repositioned. The U.S. shows up as the exporter because it’s one of the world’s main hubs for refining, vaulting, and delivery, not because Washington is choosing to send gold away.
The timing matters. These shifts don’t happen when everything feels stable. They show up alongside tighter global liquidity, slowing growth abroad, and recurring stress in weaker currencies. Gold tends to move before those pressures show up cleanly in official data. It’s more of a warning light than a confirmation.
And this is where the U.S. is structurally different. Even though gold is leaving the U.S. in the data, the U.S. itself doesn’t need to move gold to stay liquid. It already holds what everyone else is trying to get..the reserve currency and the settlement infrastructure. In a global downturn, dollars get pulled inward because debts are paid in dollars, trade is invoiced in dollars, and funding ultimately clears through the dollar system. That’s why the dollar often strengthens in recessions even when the U.S. economy is slowing.
For countries on the outside, gold is an escape hatch..a way to reduce dependence on a system where access can tighten or be revoked. For the U.S., exporting official gold would undermine confidence. The U.S. wants its reserves visible, anchored, and unquestioned. Stability is the product. What’s moving here is market gold, responding to foreign demand for control and jurisdiction.
There’s also a signaling element. When smaller or more exposed countries move gold, they’re signaling concern about future access or control. When gold flows out of the U.S. via markets while U.S. reserves stay put..it reinforces the hierarchy. The system still runs through Washington, New York, and the dollar plumbing.
The U.S. trade deficit went down. That's good for GDP. But a big part of the reason was huge gold exports. What does it say when gold is leaving the U.S. in record amounts? Is the short-term boost revealing a long-term collapse? https://t.co/VLcKEVdi8S 
- 
James Rickards

title: Greenland Is The Cover Story
content:
Greenland Is The Cover Story
I don’t think this is really about Greenland. That’s the clean, defensible headline. What matters is who is meeting..the UK, Germany, and France. That combination is about coordination among the core European powers at a moment when the Russia–Ukraine war is dragging on, risks are rising, and Europe knows it can’t stay in the passenger seat forever.
What This Coordination Is Actually Aimed At
My read is that this is about preparing Europe for deeper involvement in the Russia–Ukraine conflict without saying that out loud. Framing talks around Greenland gives political cover to do the hard work like aligning command structures, logistics, force readiness, and decision making speed. Those capabilities don’t care where they’re used. Once they exist, they can pivot north, east, or anywhere else on the map.
Europe is slowly accepting a reality it’s resisted since 2022 that supporting Ukraine indefinitely at arm’s length may not be enough, and that deterrence against Russia requires credible, coordinated European power. This isn’t about marching troops tomorrow. It’s about building the plumbing so that if escalation comes, Europe isn’t scrambling to invent coordination under fire.
There’s also a strategic pressure angle. Any serious buildup in Europe’s northern and eastern posture forces Russia to think in more than one direction. That alone changes calculations. It stretches resources, complicates planning, and raises the cost of prolonging the war. You don’t need to call that escalation for it to be effective.
The Tell
If this is just talk, it fades quietly. If it’s real, you’ll see it show up in unglamorous places like joint exercises, permanent command arrangements, pre positioned equipment, defense budgets that stop being symbolic. That’s how Europe signals it’s moving from support to participation.
So Greenland may be the excuse, but the direction of travel looks clear. This feels like Europe getting ready to be more directly involved in the Russia–Ukraine confrontation not necessarily tomorrow, but deliberately, and with fewer illusions about staying on the sidelines.

The U.S. benefits from that outcome. A more organized, self-starting Europe makes escalation less unilateral, keeps deterrence collective, and reduces the risk of NATO looking fragmented at the worst possible moment.

That dependency flips the incentive. Europe doesn’t want distance from Washington; it wants predictability and alignment. Energy, security, and finance are now tightly linked, so coordinating around Greenland reads less like brinkmanship and more like risk management, pulling the Arctic firmly inside a NATO framework, clarifying roles, and reducing ambiguity. This isn’t about crumbs or leverage against the U.S. It’s about keeping the system coherent at a moment when Europe is more exposed than it’s been in decades, which naturally pushes it closer to the U.S., not away.

title: A Prison Yard Lesson Playing Out in Real Time
content:
A Prison Yard Lesson Playing Out in Real Time
Imagine a prison yard where everyone knows who the strongest group is. Any time that group starts moving on its own, tension spikes. History says when they move first, things can spiral fast. Everyone watches closely.
So another influential group starts spreading the word…“We need to keep an eye on them. Make sure they don’t act alone.” To most inmates in the prison, it sounds like caution, like someone is trying to keep the peace by slowing the biggest player down.
But that’s only the surface story…
Behind the scenes, the strongest group has already been talking quietly with the others. They don’t fully trust each other, and they’ve clashed before, but they all see the same problem forming elsewhere in the yard…another group organizing in a way that threatens everyone’s position. No one wants to take that on alone, and no one wants to be the one who moves first and sets the whole place on edge.
So the keep an eye on them narrative becomes useful cover. The other groups start making small moves first…shifting positions, tightening space, setting conditions so the strongest group doesn’t have to act early or alone. To outsiders, it looks like supervision. Like restraint.
In reality, it’s coordination.
The strongest group isn’t being boxed in, it’s being covered. When movement finally happens, it doesn’t look like one group starting chaos. It looks collective, measured, and justified.
Same yard, same balance of power…just a different story for the people watching. That’s how talk of restraint quietly turns into alignment when everyone’s interests line up and a bigger threat has to be dealt with together.

title: Federal prosecutors in Washington have opened a cr...
content:
Federal prosecutors in Washington have opened a criminal inquiry into Fed Chair Jerome Powell tied to the huge renovation of the Federal Reserve’s headquarters. 
The question is whether Powell gave Congress misleading testimony about the scope and cost of the project. 
The renovation budget has climbed into the roughly 2.5 billion dollar range and earlier design documents appeared to include things like executive dining areas, private elevators, and other features critics call luxury upgrades.
Powell has told Congress those items were largely removed and that the project is mainly about fixing serious safety, structural and security issues in an aging building. 
Republicans and Trump allies argue the documents don’t fully match his testimony and have accused him of lying under oath, which is what triggered this referral to federal prosecutors.
At this stage, Powell has not been charged and the investigation may ultimately be closed without a case. 
But the move is still significant. 
It takes what started as a political attack over spending and turns it into a legal process inside the Justice Department. 
That alone puts a cloud over Powell’s reputation and gives his opponents an easy talking point, the Fed chair is under federal investigation.
The bigger story is how this plays into the power struggle over the Fed and interest rate policy. 
Trump has been furious that Powell has not cut rates as much or as fast as he wants and the White House has been looking for ways to pressure him or even force him out. 
The renovation fight is a convenient vehicle, it makes Powell look out of touch and potentially dishonest, and it frames the Fed as spending billions on itself while ordinary people deal with high borrowing costs.
 If the investigation drags on, it can weaken Powell’s political standing, make him more cautious, and raise questions about whether he can finish his term.
In an extreme scenario where prosecutors did bring charges, the pressure for him to resign would be intense, which could open the door for a more politically aligned replacement.
For markets, the dollars involved in the renovation are basically irrelevant but the uncertainty around Fed leadership is not.
Traders will mostly care about whether this makes a change in policy or personnel more likely.
 If investors think this increases the odds that Powell gets replaced by someone more willing to slash rates, you could see lower yields and a friendlier backdrop for risk assets.
 If it just looks like more political chaos around a key institution, it can add a bit of risk premium and volatility.

At face value, this sounds like a cool science sto...
content:
At face value, this sounds like a cool science story where researchers tweak LSD, move a couple atoms around, and end up with something that helps the brain heal without sending you on a trip. That part is real. What they’re really isolating is the part of the drug that makes the brain more flexible and less stuck in the same loops without blowing open perception. In clinical terms, that’s neuroplasticity. In human terms, it’s the ability to reset patterns that got too rigid.
But that’s also why this story connects directly to the past. The thing governments ran into with LSD wasn’t just the visuals or the chaos. It was that same flexibility. LSD turned out to be a terrible tool for control because it didn’t reliably confuse people or make them compliant. A lot of the time, it did the opposite. It made people question authority, rethink moral assumptions, feel more connected, and less willing to accept official stories at face value. What modern science now calls brain healing was, in the 1960s, a kind of cognitive solvent that spilled into culture.
That’s where figures like Ken Kesey and Timothy Leary mattered, they translated a lab phenomenon into everyday life. Once psychedelics left hospitals and universities and showed up in music, art, and protest right in the middle of Vietnam and the civil rights era the state lost control of the narrative. Psychedelics didn’t create distrust in institutions, but they lowered the barrier to seeing through contradictions at a time when trust was already thin.
So this new research isn’t just about a drug. It’s about an old tension resurfacing. Today’s version is calmer and more controlled in things like labs, trials, medical language, strict protocols. The goal is clear, keep the healing, strip out the cultural shockwave. You could read that as progress, or as refinement. Either way, it quietly confirms the same lesson learned decades ago that psychedelics aren’t reliable tools of obedience. They change how people think. And once that spreads beyond controlled settings, it tends to point in directions power doesn’t get to choose.

title: The clean way to think about it is that credit car...
content:
The clean way to think about it is that credit card rates aren’t a clean policy lever. They are technically tied to the prime rate, which follows Fed funds but the prime rate is only the base. Issuers stack a massive spread on top, often 10–20 percentage points, to cover defaults, operating costs, and profit. In 2025, that spread did all the work. Delinquencies were rising, balances were growing, and the consumer was getting weaker, not stronger. So even as the Fed cut, banks either held spreads steady or widened them. When APRs are already north of 21%, a 25 bp cut is basically noise, and banks are always faster to pass hikes through than relief.
The real issue was issuer behavior in a riskier environment. Banks didn’t read the cuts as all clear. They read them as the Fed reacting to stress. And when risk is rising, spreads dominate policy. That’s why the expected middle class relief never showed up. The Fed eased, but credit markets were already pricing for a weaker borrower, not a healthier one.

President Trump is promising affordability fixes before the midterms but most of them are impossible and will never happen.
The 10 percent credit card interest rate cap is the most politically viable, though Trump hasn't explained how he'd enforce it, executive action, voluntary pressure, or Congress.

The $200 billion mortgage bond purchase program is may actually happen.

However, if rates fall, buyers might just pay higher prices for homes since housing inventory remains constrained.
 By midterms, borrowers might see a less than quarter to half point reduction, enough for marketing but not enough to solve the housing crisis.​
The institutional investor housing ban is largely theater.

The Fed doesn't work on Trump's command, and even his new chair won't suddenly vote for reckless easing.​
Gas prices have actually fallen to sub-$2 in several states, but Trump's taking credit for something driven by OPEC+ production, not his domestic policy. 
Oil production under Trump is actually growing slower than under Biden. 
Expect him to continue marketing lower gas as his achievement, and voters might buy it simply because they're paying less at the pump.​
The $2,000 tariff stimulus checks don't add up mathematically. 
A $2,000 check for everyone earning under $100,000 would cost roughly $450 billion but tariffs are projected to raise only around $195 billion, a $255 billion shortfall. 
The Supreme Court is still deciding whether Trump's tariffs were even legal.
Don't expect actual payments before midterms.

title: Fleets don’t pull back on big ticket equipment bec...
content:
Fleets don’t pull back on big ticket equipment because they’re nervous in theory. They do it because loads are thinner, pricing power is gone, financing hurts, and cash flow matters again. By the time truck sales roll over, the goods economy is already under stress even if the broader economy hasn’t admitted it yet.
What matters here is the speed and depth of the drop. Class 8 retail sales fell hard through late 2025, down roughly 30–35% year over year by November. That’s not noise or seasonality. That’s fleets hitting pause. December orders bounced sharply, but that looks less like a clean recovery and more like pent up ordering after months of uncertainty..some catch up, some hedging against future cost increases, not a surge of confidence.
The Freight Recession Never Really Ended
The freight downturn that started in 2023 didn’t resolve in 2025 it just changed shape. Manufacturing stayed in contraction, shipment volumes remained weak, and carrier margins were under constant pressure. Yes, there were moments late in the year when spot rates and tender rejections jumped, but those spikes lined up with peak season and capacity slowly bleeding out, not a durable demand rebound.
That distinction matters. A tight week or two doesn’t fix a year of weak volumes. Fleets know the difference, which is why they’re still reluctant to commit to new iron.
Goods vs. Services Is The Quiet Structural Drag
A big part of the story is simply that the economy shifted. Services recovered faster and stayed stronger, while goods demand normalized and then stalled. GDP can look fine in that world, stock markets can levitate, and yet trucking which lives and dies on physical throughput can still be in a recession of its own.
Truck Sales Are Siding With Pallets And Factories, Not Narratives 
Labor rules tightened, but demand stayed weak
New enforcement around English language proficiency and immigration rules did sideline drivers at the margin. It added friction, paperwork, and risk. But it didn’t create a true shortage because demand wasn’t strong enough to expose one. Weak freight absorbed the supply shock. Capacity only tightens meaningfully when volumes push back, and that hasn’t happened yet in a sustained way.
Regulation, Tariffs, And Cost Uncertainty Froze Decision Making
EPA 2027 emissions rules are still coming in some form, but the details keep shifting. Add tariffs on imported trucks and components, higher interest rates, and falling used truck values, and you get paralysis. Fleets aren’t confident enough to pre buy, but they’re also wary of what future trucks might cost. So they wait. They run older equipment longer. That’s how you get collapses like the one on this chart.
My View
This is a warning from the real economy. Heavy truck sales are telling you the goods side is already behaving like it’s in a downturn. Services and financial markets are masking it for now, but history says that gap doesn’t stay open forever.
The setup for the next rebound won’t trigger until demand actually turns. Until then, this chart isn’t crying wolf. It’s saying the stress is already here, just not evenly distributed yet.

title: The U6 and U3 spread widens when employers stop ex...
content:
The U6 and U3 spread widens when employers stop expanding hours, lean harder on part time work, and downgrade roles before they ever start firing people. It’s the early, quieter phase of labor stress and the kind that doesn’t show up in the headline rate but shows up in paychecks and schedules.
Right now that gap is back above levels that usually signal comfort. The headline unemployment rate still looks fine, but under the hood more people are working fewer hours or in roles below their skill level. Historically, that’s how slowdowns surface first.
Why It’s  Happening Now
This doesn’t look like mass AI driven job destruction. The data still doesn’t support that. What it looks like is companies protecting margins in a high rate world. When capital is expensive and demand is uneven, firms try to squeeze efficiency without cutting headcount. Hours get trimmed. Hiring slows. Promotions stall. That pressure shows up in U6 long before it shows up in U3.
The sector mix matters too. Hiring is still strong in healthcare, government, and other sticky service areas, while tech, retail, and parts of white collar work are softer. That keeps the headline labor market afloat while masking weakness in more cyclical and higher paid segments.
The AI narrative Versus The Economic Reality
AI has become a convenient explanation for layoffs that are really about cost control and uncertainty. Saying AI efficiency sounds strategic. Saying demand is softer than expected doesn’t and especially in a market where a handful of AI heavy stocks carry an outsized share of index performance. When markets are this concentrated, narratives matter more than usual.
That doesn’t mean AI isn’t changing work. It is. But so far it’s reshaping tasks and leverage inside jobs more than eliminating jobs outright. The labor stress we’re seeing fits a late cycle slowdown pattern far better than a technology shock.
Where This Usually Leads
If the spread keeps widening, the next phase is typically slower hiring and, eventually, layoffs once firms realize demand isn’t coming back quickly. If it stabilizes and rolls over, it means companies successfully absorbed the slowdown through hours and productivity instead of payroll cuts.
Either way, this chart is telling you the labor market is cooling even if the headline number hasn’t caught up yet. It’s not a crisis signal but it’s not nothing either. It’s the kind of quiet warning that shows up before everyone agrees something has changed.
There's not much evidence that AI is causing unemployment yet, but there's plenty of underemployment.
The spread between the U6 and U3 unemployment rates continues to rise and is now more than 400 bps. https://t.co/FStlePKqnC 
- 
Eric Basmajian

title: On top of that, the retirement picture is a lot mo...
content:
On top of that, the retirement picture is a lot more fragile than the averages make it sound.
Boomers as a group hold a little over half of total U.S. wealth but that stat hides how uneven it really is. About 50% of people nearing or in their 70s either doubt they’ll be ready for retirement or worry their money won’t last. A third of retirees have already thought about going back to work because savings aren’t covering basics. And somewhere between a fifth and a quarter have no retirement savings at all.
Then there’s long term care, which is where the math really breaks. If you make it to 65, the odds are high you’ll need some form of care later on. A meaningful share will spend time in a nursing home or assisted living. Yet most haven’t set aside anything specifically for it, and fewer than half have a real plan. Those are costs are hard to face and harder to fund.
The wealth distribution explains the anxiety. More than 59% of peak boomers sit below $250k in total retirement assets. Only about a third are above $500k. To be genuinely comfortable like in the top decile, you’re talking roughly $3 million. Meanwhile, the bottom half of the generation holds only a sliver of the wealth, while the top 1% holds a huge chunk.
So when someone says the median 70 year old couple isn’t rich, that’s not cynicism. It’s reality. The system quietly assumes retirees can absorb shocks of inflation, healthcare, market drawdowns. For a lot of people, that cushion just isn’t there.
The median net worth of a 70-year old couple (household) in the US is $410,000. Note that "Wealth in this age group is often concentrated in home equity and retirement savings, with many still carrying some debt (e.g., mortgages or medical)."
Translation: They ain't rich. 
- 
Dave Collum

title: “If everyone is thinking alike, then somebody isn’...
content:
“If everyone is thinking alike, then somebody isn’t thinking” - General George S. Patton
•   Youth unemployment (ages 16–24):  10.4% (well above the overall U.S. unemployment rate of  4.4%, consistent with late cycle slowdowns and elevated versus most non recessionary periods).
•   Recent college graduate unemployment (ages 22–27):  4.8% (higher than during the dot com bust and roughly comparable to levels seen near the 2008–2009 GFC peak, marking a major reversal of the long standing college premium).
•   College grad vs overall unemployment gap: recent graduates now have an unemployment rate above the national average (historically rare; similar only during deep stress periods like the GFC).
•  U6–U3 underemployment spread: More than 400 basis points, a level widely associated with recessionary or post recession conditions and approaching what was seen during the Great Financial Crisis, excluding the COVID spike.
•   Involuntary part time work: nearly 1 million more people working part time for economic reasons than a year ago (a classic pre-layoff signal; elevated during the GFC).
•   Multiple job holders: 9.3 million people, a 25 year high (levels consistent with financial stress seen in past downturns, including the GFC).
•   Job quits rate: 2.0% (Nov 2025) (down sharply from the 2021 peak and back near long run averages; similar to late cycle and recessionary environments like 2008–2009).
•   Challenger job cuts (2025 YTD): tracking near the Great Financial Crisis path (explicitly comparable to GFC era cumulative layoffs, excluding the one off COVID shock).
•    Heavy truck sales: sharply declining (historically, collapses of this magnitude coincide with or precede recessions, including the GFC).
•   WTI crude oil: down 20–24% YoY (moves of this scale typically reflect weakening demand; similar declines occurred during the GFC and other growth shocks).
•   Credit card serious delinquencies (90+ days): 2.98% (Q3 2025) (above pre-pandemic levels; not yet at GFC peaks, but moving in the same late cycle direction).
•   Auto loan serious delinquencies: 2.94% (Q1 2025); new delinquencies 7.8% (Q3 2025) (trajectory consistent with consumer stress seen heading into the GFC).
•   Student loan delinquencies and defaults: 9.4% (Q3 2025) (spike following payment resumption; levels comparable to stressed credit phases, though structurally different from the GFC).
•   Commercial real estate (CRE) debt maturity wall: $1.8 trillion in 2026 (refinancing risk at rates far above origination levels; echoes the GFC mechanism, though centered on CRE rather than housing).
•   Office vacancy rate: 20.4% (Q1 2025); availability 22.8% (Q3 2025) (record highs; worse than most pre GFC readings for office real estate).
•   Industrial vacancy rate: 6.8% (late 2025) (rising and consistent with cyclical slowdown phases).
•   Bankruptcies (2025):
•   7,940 commercial Chapter 11 filings
•   2,446 Subchapter V elections
•   10,386 combined filings
(below absolute GFC peaks, but clearly trending upward in a late cycle pattern).
•   Overall picture: labor quality deteriorating, layoffs accelerating, goods demand weakening, credit stress rising, and CRE refinancing risk mounting, a combination that has historically only appeared near or inside recessions, most notably during the Great Financial Crisis.

BLS Employment Situation In December 2025 And Reading Past the Noise
The unemployment rate is just unemployed divided by the labor force. In December, the number of unemployed fell by 278k, while employment rose 232k and the labor force slipped 46k. That combination mechanically pushes the rate down (from 4.5% to 4.4%). The “improvement” is mostly a numerator story (fewer counted as unemployed) with a small assist from the denominator (a slightly smaller labor force).  
Then read the footnotes (where the real story lives)
Two things matter here if you’re being skeptical…
•   Seasonal adjustment got revised. BLS updated seasonal factors and revised household survey history. Notably, November’s unemployment rate was revised down (4.6 to 4.5). So part of the drop people see is revision plus seasonality, not some dramatic new shift in December.
•   This is household survey territory, it’s noisy. BLS basically tells you this in the technical note: the monthly change in the unemployment rate has a confidence interval on the order of ±0.2 percentage point. A 0.1 move is not a clean signal. It’s a watch it, not a declare it. 
If You’re Hunting Recession Fingerprints, Don’t Stare At U-3
The recessionary tells in this report aren’t the headline rate, they’re the quality and persistence underneath it…
•   Underemployment is elevated. People working part time for economic reasons are 5.3M, and that’s up 980k over the year. That’s employers and workers meeting each other at the margin, not in confident full time hiring.  
•   Hidden slack is growing. People not in the labor force who currently want a job are 6.2M, up 684k over the year. That’s the quiet way labor markets weaken: more people want work, but they’re not counted in U-3 because they aren’t “actively”searching in the last 4 weeks.  
•   Long term unemployment is creeping. Long term unemployed are 1.9M, up 397k over the year, and they’re 26% of all unemployed. That’s a classic late cycle deterioration: hiring slows, and unemployment becomes stickier.  
•   Broader measures still look worse than a year ago. Even though they improved a bit in December, U-6 is 8.4% (vs 7.6% a year ago), and U-4/U-5 follow the same better this month, worse over the year pattern.  
The Payroll Survey Is Waving A Bigger Red Flag Than The Unemployment Rate
Payrolls were +50k and BLS basically says you can’t hang your hat on that month to month: the confidence band for monthly payroll change is large enough that +50k can still be no change statistically.  
The more important tells…
•   The 3 month average payroll change is negative (about ‑22k). That’s stall speed.
•   Revisions went the wrong way. October and November were revised down (combined ‑76k). In turning points, revisions often betray the initial optimism.  
•   Sector mix looks defensive. Gains are concentrated in food services, health care, social assistance while retail trade lost 25k and areas like transport and warehousing and temp help are weak. That’s households still spending, but the goods and credit cycle is tightening.  
•Hours are slipping. The workweek edged down, and the aggregate hours index fell. In real downturns, employers usually cut hours first, then heads. This is the early part of that movie.

Federal government employment down 277k since January (‑9.2%) is a huge swing and the report explicitly notes that people on paid leave or ongoing severance can still be counted as employed in the establishment survey. Essentially some labor market pain can get time shifted in how it shows up.

title: This Chart Explains Why the Economy Feels Off
content:
This Chart Explains Why the Economy Feels Off
This chart isn’t about a bad quarter or a quirky data revision. It’s showing a long, structural shift. For decades after World War II, workers reliably took a little over 60% of the economic pie. That wasn’t accidental. It reflected strong unions, tighter regulation, limited globalization, and a system that funneled productivity gains back into wages.
That floor started cracking in the 1980s. It never truly came back. And over the last twenty years especially after 2000 the decline stopped being cyclical and became structural. The latest reading just makes that impossible to ignore. Labor’s share isn’t low relative to the past few years. It’s low relative to modern U.S. history.
This isn’t about workers suddenly becoming less productive. Productivity has actually been decent. The problem is that productivity gains aren’t flowing to paychecks. They’re flowing to margins.
Why This Keeps Happening
The story underneath is bargaining power. Globalization, automation, weaker labor institutions, and rising market concentration all tilt leverage away from workers. Large, dominant firms can scale without hiring much labor. Care and service jobs add headcount, but they don’t reset wage power across the economy. So employment can grow while labor’s slice shrinks.
Policy matters here too, but not always in the way people think. Asset supportive policies helped stabilize the economy after crises, but they also boosted capital values much faster than wages. That cushions downturns without fixing distribution. Over time, that gap compounds.
You can see it in the data around this chart with weak hiring momentum, more people working multiple jobs, slower real wage growth, and profits holding up fine. That combination almost guarantees downward pressure on labor share.
What It Means For The Economy
A falling labor share doesn’t just show up as inequality. It changes how the economy behaves. When income shifts toward capital, spending becomes more fragile. Growth leans harder on credit, fiscal support, or asset wealth effects. Things can look stable on the surface while feeling tight underneath.
Markets often like this setup at first. Lower labor costs support margins. Inflation stays contained. Stocks do fine. But over time, revenue growth gets harder if workers can’t keep spending. And eventually the imbalance shows up somewhere else…politically, socially, or financially.
My View
This chart isn’t a warning about tomorrow. It’s a diagnosis of the system we’re already in. Productivity is still there. Growth is still possible. But the link between economic gains and worker pay has weakened to a degree we haven’t seen before.
That doesn’t break the economy overnight. It slowly changes its character. And history says that when labor’s share gets this low, it stops being just an economic statistic and starts becoming a macro force of its own.

title: An underemployment rate of 41.8% for recent colleg...
content:
An underemployment rate of 41.8% for recent college graduates means more than four in ten are either unemployed or working jobs that don’t really match their education. For context, the dot com bust peaked around 38.5% in late 2002, after tech hiring froze. During COVID, the rate briefly jumped to about 43.2%, but that was a sudden shutdown followed by a rapid reopening. The Great Financial Crisis was worse, underemployment for recent grads ultimately pushed close to 50%, but crucially, that peak didn’t arrive until years after the recession officially began.
What’s unsettling now is the timing. We’re already above dot com levels and not far from COVID peaks, without an officially declared recession and while headline unemployment still looks fine 
🧐
🤔
Historically, that only happens when hiring has quietly broken first. Firms don’t start by firing experienced workers; they stop hiring, freeze entry level roles, and downgrade jobs. New grads feel it immediately. Either hiring rebounds hard from here, or this is doing what it’s usually done in the past, flagging a labor market that’s weaker than it looks before the broader data catches up.
Underemployment rate for recent college graduates rose to 41.8%, per New York Fed.
